A few of the posts on this blog lean on the same small trick: a function written inside a pandas chain, so that one step can see what the step before it just built. It works, it is short, and reading it does not tell you why it is there.

pandas 3 has a shorter way to write it. This post takes three snippets I published here, runs them again exactly as they were written, and then does the same jobs with `pd.col()` so the two can be put side by side. Every code block below runs when this page is built, and the output under it is what the code printed.

## First, what a lambda is

A lambda is a function written where it is used, without a name:

::: {#8776a45a .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
double = lambda x: x * 2

def double_named(x):
    return x * 2

print(double(21), double_named(21))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
42 42
```
:::
:::


Same job, two spellings. The only reason to reach for the first is that it fits inside another call, which is somewhere a `def` statement cannot go. That is the whole idea.

In pandas it turns up for a less obvious reason. When pandas runs a method, it works out the arguments first and then runs the method. Inside a chain, the frame that a step is about to produce does not exist yet at that moment. A lambda puts the calculation off until the step is actually running, when the frame does exist.

## The trick, from the 2024 post

This is the one I wrote about in [Lambda Functions: How I tend to use them](https://www.sisengai.com/blog/2024-May-25-Lambda-Functions/lambda_functions.html), using the same CSV that post used. Here it is again, unchanged:

::: {#a132b13f .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd

def tweak_data(url):
    return (pd.read_csv(url)
            .assign(Date=lambda x: pd.to_datetime(x['Date']),
                    Month=lambda x: x['Date'].dt.month_name()))

data = tweak_data('synthetic_stock_data.csv')
print(data.head(3).to_string(index=False))
print()
print(data.dtypes.to_string())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
      Date       Close   Month
2023-01-02 3773.956049 January
2023-01-03 3438.878440 January
2023-01-04 3858.597920 January

Date     datetime64[us]
Close           float64
Month               str
```
:::
:::


Look at the second line. `Month` reads the `Date` column, and that column only becomes a date on the line above — inside the same `assign` call. Both lines are the same call, so nothing is committed until the call runs. Writing it without the lambda, as most people first try, does not work:

::: {#ca28c96e .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# the same lines without a lambda, the way most people first write it
raw = pd.read_csv('synthetic_stock_data.csv')
try:
    raw.assign(Date=pd.to_datetime(raw['Date']),
               Month=raw['Date'].dt.month_name())
except AttributeError as exc:
    print(type(exc).__name__, "-", exc)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
AttributeError - Can only use .dt accessor with datetimelike values
```
:::
:::


The same post used a second pattern, a lambda handed to `agg` so that each group is reduced by my own calculation:

::: {#0b65119a .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

print(data
 .groupby('Month')
 ['Close']
 .agg(lambda x: np.percentile(x, 25))
 .round(2)
 .to_string())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

## The same trick in two other posts

Lambdas show up in the [Karachi property prices post](https://www.sisengai.com/blog/2024-January-04-Karachi-Property-Prices/KarachiPropertyPrices.html) too, where they clean column names and split a price into a number and a currency. That post read a CSV of its own, so here is the same code on three rows in the same shape:

::: {#49c5b303 .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
karachi = pd.DataFrame({
    "property type": ["Flat", "House", "Plot"],
    "price": ["2.5 Crore PKR", "4 Crore PKR", "75 Lakh PKR"],
})

print(karachi
 .rename(columns=lambda x: x.replace(" ", "_"))
 .assign(price_=lambda x: x["price"].str.split(" ", expand=True)[0],
         currency_name=lambda x: x["price"].str.split(" ", expand=True)[1])
 .astype({"price_": float})
 .to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
property_type         price  price_ currency_name
         Flat 2.5 Crore PKR     2.5         Crore
        House   4 Crore PKR     4.0         Crore
         Plot   75 Lakh PKR    75.0          Lakh
```
:::
:::


And in the [weather data wrangling post](https://www.sisengai.com/blog/2023-December-27-Data-Wrangling/Data_Wrangling.html), the same `assign` shape appears one more time — a date column converted, then a month number taken from the column that conversion just made:

::: {#a7b8c71b .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
bikes = pd.DataFrame({
    "dteday": ["2011-01-01", "2011-02-14", "2011-03-09"],
    "hum": [0.81, 0.80, 0.63],
})

print(bikes
 .assign(dteday=pd.to_datetime(bikes['dteday']),
         mnth=lambda x: x['dteday'].dt.month)
 .to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
    dteday  hum  mnth
2011-01-01 0.81     1
2011-02-14 0.80     2
2011-03-09 0.63     3
```
:::
:::


Three posts, one pattern: convert something, then use the result of the conversion in the same call. The lambda is what makes the second half possible.

## What was going on

The lambda is not a loop, and that matters. It is called **once**, with the whole frame as its argument, and inside that call `x['Date']` is a full column — the arithmetic runs on the column, at pandas speed. A lambda handed to `.apply()` row by row is a different animal entirely: that one is Python running per row and it is slow. The chain lambdas in these posts are the fast kind.

The reason they are needed at all is ordering. pandas evaluates the arguments of a method before it runs that method. In a chain, the value being built is not available to its own arguments yet. So the lambda is a way of saying *calculate this later, when the frame is ready*. It is handed the frame as the chain has built it so far, which is why a chain that renames columns first has to reach the new names through a lambda.

## The same three jobs with pd.col

pandas 3 adds a second way to say exactly that. `pd.col("name")` is not the column; it is a stand-in for a column — the documentation calls it "a deferred object representing a column of a DataFrame", and anywhere that accepts `lambda df: df[col_name]` will also accept `pd.col(col_name)`.

Here are the three snippets again, written that way:

::: {#94dcbd8d .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def tweak_data_v3(url):
    return (pd.read_csv(url, parse_dates=["Date"])
            .assign(Month=pd.col("Date").dt.month_name()))

new = tweak_data_v3('synthetic_stock_data.csv')
print(new.head(3).to_string(index=False))
print()
print("same result as the lambda version:", new.equals(data))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
      Date       Close   Month
2023-01-02 3773.956049 January
2023-01-03 3438.878440 January
2023-01-04 3858.597920 January

same result as the lambda version: True
```
:::
:::


The column is named once — `pd.col("Date")` — instead of being named once for the frame and again inside the function body.

The second snippet needs a correction, and it is a useful one. That `agg(lambda ...)` was never doing the deferral job at all. `agg` hands each group to the function one at a time, so a lambda there is just a small function, and `np.percentile` with its own keyword does the same work. What the two lines below check is that the numbers are identical either way:

::: {#9470e913 .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
old_months = (data.groupby('Month')['Close']
              .agg(lambda x: np.percentile(x, 25)).round(2))
new_months = (data.groupby('Month')['Close']
              .agg(np.percentile, q=25).round(2))
print("quarterly percentiles identical:", old_months.equals(new_months))
print(new_months.to_string())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
quarterly percentiles identical: True
Month
April        3245.80
August       3268.60
December     3247.84
February     3226.91
January      3165.53
July         3331.57
June         3183.17
March        3323.71
May          3269.06
November     3290.07
October      3183.56
September    3240.97
```
:::
:::


::: {#3123b922 .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
v3_bikes = (bikes
            .assign(dteday=pd.to_datetime(bikes['dteday']))
            .assign(mnth=pd.col("dteday").dt.month))

with_lambda = (bikes
               .assign(dteday=pd.to_datetime(bikes['dteday']),
                       mnth=lambda x: x['dteday'].dt.month))

print("month column identical:", v3_bikes["mnth"].tolist() == with_lambda["mnth"].tolist())
print("both month columns:", with_lambda["mnth"].tolist())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
month column identical: True
both month columns: [1, 2, 3]
```
:::
:::


The third snippet is where `pd.col()` earns its place, because there the lambda really was postponing the calculation. Nothing is delayed with `pd.col("dteday")`, so the line reads in the order it runs, and the conversion is separated from the step that uses its result — which is what makes the failure in the earlier section impossible to write by accident.

## Where pd.col does not help

It is not a replacement for every lambda in those posts. The `rename(columns=...)` lambda has no equivalent, because `rename` is not working on a frame's contents — it is working on the labels:

::: {#8b202a42 .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
try:
    karachi.rename(columns=pd.col("property type"))
except TypeError as exc:
    print(type(exc).__name__, "-", " ".join(str(exc).split()))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
TypeError - boolean value of an expression is ambiguous
```
:::
:::


The same wall shows up with functions rather than labels. A NumPy function composes with an expression and hands back the column asked for; anything that has to inspect the expression while the chain is still being built refuses:

::: {#df389805 .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
frame = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 4, 9, 16]})

try:
    frame.assign(band=pd.cut(pd.col("a"), bins=2))
except TypeError as exc:
    print("pd.cut with pd.col:", type(exc).__name__, "-", " ".join(str(exc).split()))

print(frame.assign(log_a=np.round(np.log(pd.col("a")), 3)).to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
pd.cut with pd.col: TypeError - boolean value of an expression is ambiguous
 a  log_a
 1  0.000
 4  1.386
 9  2.197
16  2.773
```
:::
:::


So the rule is narrower than "it does not work everywhere". `pd.col()` is an expression that has not been evaluated yet: anything that only needs the column's **values** can write it — arithmetic, NumPy, the `.str` and `.dt` accessors — and anything that needs a yes-or-no answer about the expression while the chain is being built cannot, which is exactly what `pd.cut` and `rename` have in common. The release notes for 3.0 call this "initial support" and name three places it works — `assign`, `loc`, and setting by column — so it is early.

## What else changed in pandas 3

Three things worth knowing before the next run of an old notebook, in case the reader hits them at the same time:

::: {#4edfd5ba .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
print("a string column now reports:", pd.Series(["a", "b"]).dtype)
print("the old default was:", pd.Series(["a", "b"], dtype=object).dtype)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
a string column now reports: str
the old default was: object
```
:::
:::


::: {#271a7f21 .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import warnings

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [10, 20, 30]})
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    df["a"][df["b"] > 15] = 99

print("warning:", caught[0].category.__name__ if caught else "none")
print("the write did not land:", df.to_dict("records"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
warning: ChainedAssignmentError
the write did not land: [{'a': 1, 'b': 10}, {'a': 2, 'b': 20}, {'a': 3, 'b': 30}]
```
:::
:::


There is a second half to the strings change. The default `str` dtype reports missing values as `NaN`, and a comparison against a value treats them as unequal; the nullable dtype keeps the answer missing instead:

::: {#9da53a09 .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code}
dogs = pd.Series(["dog", None])
print("default str dtype:", list(dogs == "dog"))
print("nullable dtype   :", list(pd.Series(["dog", None], dtype="string") == "dog"))
print("both find it     :", list(dogs.isna()))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
default str dtype: [True, False]
nullable dtype   : [np.True_, <NA>]
both find it     : [False, True]
```
:::
:::


In the nullable dtype the comparison stays missing instead — pandas is saying it does not know whether that entry was `dog`. For code that counts rows matching a value, that is a changed answer rather than a style note.

Text columns no longer report as `object` — they report as `str`. And a two-step write, `df["a"][df["b"] > 15] = 99`, no longer writes anything: pandas warns and the frame is left alone. The single-step `df.loc[df["b"] > 15, "a"] = 99` is what works now. A defensive `.copy()` is no longer needed when its only purpose was to quiet that warning, though it still earns its place when the intent is a genuinely independent frame.

One more change belongs in that list, because it is the only one here that stops the notebook rather than warning it. The period codes were renamed: month-end `"M"` is now `"ME"`, quarter-end `"Q"` is `"QE"`, year-end `"Y"` is `"YE"`, and the business variants follow — `"BM"` → `"BME"`, `"BQ"` → `"BQE"`, `"BY"` → `"BYE"`. The minute and hour codes are `"min"` and `"h"` now:

::: {#050aeb71 .cell execution_count=15}
``` {.python .cell-code}
series = pd.Series(range(10), index=pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=10, freq="D"))

for code in ["M", "ME", "W", "T", "min"]:
    try:
        out = series.resample(code).sum()
        print("resample('" + code + "') ->", len(out), "bucket(s), first value:", out.iloc[0])
    except ValueError as exc:
        print("resample('" + code + "') ->", type(exc).__name__ + ":", str(exc).split(". ")[0])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
resample('M') -> ValueError: Invalid frequency: M
resample('ME') -> 1 bucket(s), first value: 45
resample('W') -> 2 bucket(s), first value: 21
resample('T') -> ValueError: Invalid frequency: T
resample('min') -> 12961 bucket(s), first value: 0
```
:::
:::


An old monthly `resample("M")` raises `ValueError` and the cell stops; `"ME"` gives the same answer the old code used to. Weekly and daily codes were not touched — `"W"` and `"D"` work as before — and the error message names the alias it will not accept.
